issues.location: "Two accounts, two locks, one bug" section, the `transfer-naive` code block and the sentence immediately after it: "The CountdownEvent guarantees both threads are already holding their first account's lock before either reaches for the second."
issues.problem: This is false as written. `bothStarted.Signal(); bothStarted.Wait();` sits *before* `lock (from.Gate)` in `Transfer`, not inside it (contrast with the `deadlock` and `ring` blocks earlier, where the equivalent barrier call is the first statement *inside* the first `lock`). Because of that placement, the thread that is released from the CountdownEvent without ever blocking (whichever thread calls `Signal()` last) can acquire its own lock and successfully `TryEnter` the other account's lock before the other thread — which really did block on `Wait()` and needs an OS wake-up — has acquired its own lock at all. I verified this is a real, reproducible race, not a theoretical nitpick: running the unmodified `Transfer`/threading logic in a loop, only 1 of 300 trials (with a 200ms TryEnter timeout) and 2 of 30 trials (with the article's actual 1-second timeout) produced a stall; the other ~93-99% of trials completed both transfers with no deadlock and `stalled` staying `False`. By contrast, the same stress test applied to the `deadlock` block's barrier-inside-lock pattern produced a deadlock 30/30 times. The article's own text explains, two sections earlier, exactly why the barrier must be inside the lock ('bothHolding.Wait() is what makes this reproduce every time rather than most of the time... With it, thread A cannot proceed past the barrier until it already holds lockA') — and then does not apply that lesson to this section, while claiming the same 'guarantee' anyway. In practice this section still passes `run-code.mjs` reliably (5/5 fresh-process runs for me) because a single cold `dotnet run` process happens to resolve the race toward deadlock most of the time, which is not the same thing as the stated guarantee.
issues.fixLooksLike: Move `bothStarted.Signal(); bothStarted.Wait();` to be the first statement inside `lock (from.Gate)` in both `Transfer` (naive and fixed versions), exactly matching the pattern already used correctly in the `deadlock` and `ring` blocks. Re-verify the output block afterward (still expected to be `a transfer stalled: True` / `False` respectively, but now actually guaranteed by construction rather than usually true). Alternatively, if the barrier position is kept as-is for some other reason, soften 'guarantees' to something accurate ('makes both threads start at the same moment, which on this machine reliably produces the deadlock below — though unlike the lockA/lockB version above, this isn't forced by construction') and don't claim the same certainty as the earlier, correctly-built demos.

issues.location: Every `lock` example in the article (`lock (gate) { counter++; }`, `lock (lockA)`, `lock (first.Gate)`, etc.) uses `object gate = new();` / `object lockA = new();` / `public readonly object Gate = new();`.
issues.problem: The article's own cited source, the 'lock statement' Microsoft Learn page, states in its Guidelines section: 'Starting with .NET 9 and C# 13, lock a dedicated object instance of the System.Threading.Lock type for best performance,' and its own worked example now uses `System.Threading.Lock` rather than `object` ('Use object in versions earlier than C# 13'). A second Microsoft Learn page (Managed Threading Basics) repeats the same guidance in an admonition. This article's toolchain is .NET 10.0.401 (confirmed via `dotnet --version`), which is well past the .NET 9/C# 13 threshold, yet `System.Threading.Lock` is never mentioned or used anywhere in the article, including in the 'What locking costs' section, which is specifically about lock overhead — exactly where the newer type's performance benefit would be most relevant to demonstrate or at least name. This isn't a runtime bug (the code as written is correct and runs), but it fails the brief's 'modern idiomatic C#, .NET 10' bar and teaches a pattern the article's own source says is no longer the recommended one for this toolchain.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either switch the lock objects to `System.Threading.Lock` (e.g. `System.Threading.Lock gate = new();`) and note briefly that this is the modern .NET 9+/C# 13+ recommendation over a plain `object`, or, if `object` is kept deliberately for broader applicability, add one sentence acknowledging `System.Threading.Lock` exists and is now preferred, citing the same lock-statement page already in the sources list.
